title: Egusi Soup
subtitle: West African melon seed soup with beef and spinach
excerpt: Egusi soup is one of the most popular soups across West Africa. Ground melon seeds thicken the soup and give it a distinctive rich, nutty flavour. It is cooked with beef, leafy greens, and a deep palm-oil base. It is substantial food -- closer to a stew than a soup.
sourceNotes: Egusi soup is eaten widely across West Africa, particularly in Nigeria, Ghana, Cameroon, and Sierra Leone. Egusi seeds are the dried seeds of watermelon or other cucurbits, ground to a coarse powder. Palm oil is the traditional cooking fat and gives the soup its characteristic orange-red colour.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes well for up to 2 months. Reheat gently, adding a little water to loosen.

content.text: Ground egusi seeds can be found in African food shops. If unavailable, ground pumpkin seeds make the closest substitute. Red palm oil is the traditional fat here -- it gives the soup its orange colour and a distinct earthy flavour. Regular vegetable oil works if palm oil is not available.

items.prepNote: use red palm oil for authentic colour and flavour

content.text: Season the beef with salt. Heat the oil in a large pot over high heat. Brown the beef in batches for 3 to 4 minutes. Remove and set aside.
In the same oil, cook the onion for 6 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and chilli. Cook 2 minutes.
Blend the tinned tomatoes and pour them into the pot. Cook for 10 minutes, stirring often, until the sauce darkens and thickens.
Mix the ground egusi with enough water to make a thick paste. Drop spoonfuls into the tomato sauce. Stir gently. The egusi will clump at first -- this is normal.
Return the beef to the pot. Pour in the stock. Cover and simmer for 25 minutes until the beef is tender.
Add the drained spinach. Stir through and cook for 5 more minutes. Taste and adjust salt. Serve with pounded yam, fufu, or rice.

items.cause: This is natural -- the egusi cooks into lumps
items.fix: Break up large lumps with a spoon as the soup simmers; smaller pieces are fine and add texture

items.cause: Egusi absorbs a lot of liquid
items.fix: Add more stock or water in small amounts and stir until you reach the consistency you want
Continue simmering, covered, for another 15 to 20 minutes

content.text: Egusi soup is at the heart of Nigerian, Ghanaian, and Cameroonian cooking. It is served at ceremonies, restaurants, and in homes. It is eaten with fufu, pounded yam, or rice. The ground seeds are a uniquely West African ingredient with no close equivalent elsewhere -- they give egusi soup a flavour that cannot be replicated with any substitute.
